texts: bad: the two seasons end up stacked on one habitual hunt, so each sky-cat's single hunting event is placed in summer and in early autumn at once; there is no way to split a coordinated time phrase inside one generic rule, so the seasonal information is exactly what gets dropped. Give each season its own sentence: "Sky-cats hunt often in summer. Sky-cats hunt often in early autumn." Each then parses as its own fireable rule carrying a single time.
good. the habitual routes to a fireable rule, "rarely" sets the strength and is recorded as the quantifier word, and "deep winter" rides the time slot cleanly.
good. "resume hunting" parses on the inception pattern, with the hunting attached as the ongoing activity and "in spring" in the time slot.

bad: "other insects" states an exclusion the translator has no way to record, so the safest reading drops the whole hunting claim rather than assert the wider "insects", and the phrase also pushed the parse into minting one particular insect per sky-cat instead of insects as a kind. Write the object as a plain kind: "When nightmoths are scarce, sky-cats sometimes hunt insects." If the contrast with nightmoths matters, name the substitute prey in a sentence of its own, because an "other X" phrase cannot be carried in any wording.

bad: the object stacks a nominalized "hunts" with "sky-cat" as its unstated subject and "of other insects" as its object, a shape we cannot encode, so the parse ended up asserting a free-standing generalization that sky-cats hunt insects, which your sentence only reports the logs as recording; "other" is again uncarriable. Make the recorded content a finite clause: "Marra Tallowhand's logs record that sky-cats hunt insects." The hunting is then held as what the logs say rather than asserted as a fact about sky-cats, and the prey kinds can be named separately if the exclusion matters.

bad: nothing composes a kind subject with a possessed predicate nominal, so "the sky-cats'" never reaches the predication: the parse asserts flatly that nightmoths are main food and hangs the sky-cats off the bare kind "main food", which would make anything else typed that way theirs too. Turn it into a verbal claim with both kinds as arguments: "Sky-cats usually eat nightmoths." That records the sky-cat/nightmoth relation and carries "main" through the frequency reading; the continuation sense of "remain" has no carrier for a kind-level claim and will be lost whatever the wording.
